content.text: Meet Dr. Nancy Grace Roman

content.alt_text: A black and white, waist-up portrait of a woman with short white hair wearing glasses and a floral shirt. Part of a spacecraft model is visible in front of her. It looks like a long open soup can with a metal flap on the top and several metal pieces extending from the sides. Credit: AIP Emilio Segrè Visual Archives, Roman Collection

content.text: A photo of Dr. Nancy Grace Roman holding a model of the Hubble Space Telescope.

You have to be a pretty big deal for NASA to name a space telescope after you, and that is certainly the case for Dr. Nancy Grace Roman — our Roman Space Telescope’s namesake. She’s sometimes called the “mother of Hubble,” but she’s really the mother of all space-based observatories and NASA science in general. As NASA’s first chief astronomer, Dr. Roman's vision and leadership supercharged space science and helped make NASA the world-class scientific institution it is today.

content.alt_text: A sepia-toned photo of a young girl with shoulder-length hair standing in front of a vehicle. Credit: Courtesy of Dr. Nancy Grace Roman

content.text: Nancy Grace Roman as a young child.

Nancy Grace Roman was born on May 16, 1925 in Nashville, Tennessee. She was naturally curious about the world, a trait she attributed to taking nature walks with her mother as a child. By seventh grade, she had decided that she was going to be an astronomer.
She later recounted, “I certainly did not receive any encouragement. I was told from the beginning that women could not be scientists.”

content.alt_text: A black and white photo of Dr. Nancy Grace Roman looking upward toward a wall covered in panels and buttons. Credit: AIP Emilio Segrè Visual Archives, Roman Collection

content.text: A 1972 photo of Dr. Roman at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md.

Nancy received her bachelor’s in astronomy from Swarthmore College in 1946 and her doctorate in astronomy from the University of Chicago in 1949. She specialized in spectral classification, which involves spreading starlight out into a rainbow to see the individual colors. She would decode these rainbows to learn about the temperature and brightness of the stars, and their distances and movements.

In 1959, just six months after NASA was founded, someone at the agency asked Dr. Roman if she knew someone who might be interested in creating a space-based astronomy program. She sure did — she applied for the job herself, and she got it!

content.alt_text: A black and white headshot of a woman with short hair and glasses. She’s holding a spacecraft model. Credit: AIP Emilio Segrè Visual Archives, Roman Collection

content.text: Dr. Roman works with a model of the Orbiting Solar Observatory (OSO).
Creating a whole space program from scratch was no small feat. Dr. Roman quickly set her sights on the stars, determined to make space-based telescopes a reality.

Scientists had been batting around the idea of Hubble for generations. Today, after more than three decades in orbit and thousands of discoveries, it’s hard to believe that Hubble was ever a contentious idea. But in the mid-20th century, a budget-starved NASA and a post-World War II government were hesitant to follow the ambitious ideal of a giant new telescope.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/8D6OYcQJI7k?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="NASA Names Upcoming Telescope to Honor the 'Mother of Hubble'"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: NASA Goddard - NASA Names Upcoming Telescope to Honor the 'Mother of Hubble'

content.text: But Dr. Roman knew how transformative it would be to observe the cosmos from above Earth’s turbulent atmosphere, which blurs images from even the best ground-based telescopes. So she gathered astronomers from around the country and sat them down in a room with NASA engineers to hash out the possibilities.

Then she championed the idea to Congress, saying that “for the price of one night at the movies each year, each American would receive 15 years of exciting discoveries.” (And she actually undersold it, since we’ve now received over 36 years of discoveries from Hubble!)

content.alt_text: A black and white photo of Dr. Roman surrounded by a group of female college students. They’re gathered around the edge of a table, on which there are a couple of spacecraft models — one small and wide and one tall and thin. Credit: AIP Emilio Segrè Visual Archives, Roman Collection

content.text: In this 1965 photo, Dr. Roman (center) conducts a demonstration with Smith College students during a visit to NASA.

With leadership experience stretching back to at least the fifth or sixth grade, when she organized her friends into an astronomy club, Dr. Roman paired a personable approach with unwavering commitment to the mission, regardless of who or what stood in her way. And now we have her to thank for not just Hubble but for every other space telescope that has followed.

content.alt_text: A waist-up black and white photo of a woman with short hair and glasses. In the background, a white balloon extends upward from a long tether. Credit: AIP Emilio Segrè Visual Archives, Roman Collection

content.text: A portrait of Dr. Roman with the Stratoscope II balloon in the background.

In less than a month, the observatory named in Dr. Roman’s honor will journey to the heavens to transform our view of the universe. Read more about the woman behind the mission’s name here: https://science.nasa.gov/people/nancy-roman/. Follow along with Roman’s road to launch at nasa.gov/roman, and virtually tour the Roman observatory here.

summary: Meet Dr. Nancy Grace Roman

content.text: Listen to the Sounds of Space

In movies like The Wizard of Oz and Pleasantville, characters step out of a muted, black-and-white world into one full of rich, vibrant colors. Experts at NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and elsewhere around the agency have figured out how to do something similar by translating data into sound, creating “sonifications” that allow you to more fully immerse yourself in the cosmos. Ready to dive in?

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/urmFYr2GJHE?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Sonification of Arp 140"></iframe>

content.text: If you’ve ever gazed up at the Moon or stars, you’ve likely felt a visceral sense of awe and wonder, or perhaps a profound connection with the cosmos. Turning observational data from our telescopes into corresponding frequencies can open up a similar experience to those who are blind or low-vision, while enriching the experience for others, too. The results range from celestial and ethereal to mystical and otherworldly — sometimes downright spooky!

content.embed_html: <iframe width="267" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ayAYDVvjs_E?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Data Sonification: M16 (Eagle Nebula, "Pillars of Creation") Multiwavelength"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: Chandra X-ray Observatory - Data Sonification: M16 (Eagle Nebula, "Pillars of Creation") Multiwavelength

content.text: Turning data into sound may seem unconventional, but it’s really not that different from the data visualization most of us are accustomed to. Every image from a space telescope is an extension of what we’re able to discern via human senses. Scientists often use special filters and data processing techniques to make subtle features in the data easier to study and interpret.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/j9shIxS-W-8?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Webb Telescope Data, Translated to Sound — Cosmic Cliffs in the Carina Nebula"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) - Webb Telescope Data, Translated to Sound — Cosmic Cliffs in the Carina Nebula

content.text: Only a small portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, the full range of light, is visible to the human eye. But many telescopes are designed to capture other wavelengths of light, like our Chandra X-ray Observatory and our James Webb Space Telescope, which views infrared light. Visualizations and sonifications are key to translating the data they send back into forms we can perceive and interpret. Both give us more ways to understand what our telescopes are detecting.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/_cPRrwxX8lU?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Synthetic Supernova Timelapse Sonification"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: NASA Video - Synthetic Supernova Timelapse Sonification

content.text: You may be more familiar with the concept than you think! You probably associate “radio” with sound, right? But radio waves are just another form of light. When you tune your radio to a specific frequency, it picks up those electromagnetic waves and turns the information they carry into vibrations in the speaker, creating the sound waves you can hear.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="267" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ioR5np1fmEc?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Data Sonification: Black Hole at the Center of the Perseus Galaxy Cluster (X-ray)"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center - Data Sonification: Black Hole at the Center of the Perseus Galaxy Cluster (X-ray)

content.text: Usually the cosmic objects featured in a sonification aren’t actually creating sound. But sometimes they really do! A black hole sound machine in the middle of the Perseus galaxy cluster sends pressure waves rippling out into the cluster’s hot gas. The gas is dense enough that sound waves can travel through it, creating a note humans can’t hear (some 57 octaves below middle C). But with help from a good cosmic DJ, we can bring that note into the range of human hearing.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/w8rr5lDOnlY?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Sonification of NGC 1569"></iframe>

content.text: Sonifications aren’t just for scientists. You can make one yourself! Hearing Hubble allows you to choose from 10 breathtaking views from our Hubble Space Telescope. You pick the instruments, scanning pattern, harmony, and scientific information you want to use to create a symphony that represents the image in sound! When you’re done composing, share your masterpiece on social media and with family and friends.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/vyvoewG9YU4?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Data Sonification: Uranus, Composite"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: Chandra X-ray Observatory - Data Sonification: Uranus, Composite

content.text: Still haven't gotten your fill? You can explore more NASA sonifications and listen to a NASA+ episode about sonifications. To hear more about the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, check out the special series our Curious Universe podcast is releasing!

content.text: Liftoff: Roman is Heading to L2!

content.alt_text: In a sepia-toned photo, the Sun appears as a bright, enormous orb that appears to have frayed edges. Against this backdrop, a tall and slender rocket is seen in silhouette atop a cloudy plume. Credit: NASA/John Kraus

content.text: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Sunday, Aug. 30.
Our Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is space-bound following a successful launch from our Kennedy Space Center this morning.

Now, the observatory is on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, where its mission to reveal the universe’s darkest secrets will begin. With Roman’s big-picture view of the universe, it will deliver sights we’ve never seen before and enable cosmic investigations that wouldn’t be possible without it.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/CDwemQH2zDU?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Everything You Need To Know About NASA's Roman Space Telescope"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: NASA Goddard - Everything You Need To Know About NASA's Roman Space Telescope

content.text: Roman’s launch brings us much closer to a completely new understanding of the universe and our place within it. Rather than focusing on individual objects, Roman will capture whole cosmic ecosystems. It will be a discovery machine, with so many stars and galaxies packed into each observation that we’re bound to find things we never even knew existed.

The mission pairs a large field of view with crisp infrared vision to explore vast swaths of the sky and probe deeply into cosmic history. This flagship mission is designed to help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, worlds outside of our solar system, and so much more.

content.alt_text: An animation starting with a view of Earth seen from space. A small dot labeled Roman emerges from behind it and moves toward the camera and the view zooms out as Roman races away. It travels past the Moon’s orbit and finally reaches a point labeled L2 and begins orbiting around it. Credit: NASA

content.text: This visualization shows the path Roman will take to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2). The visualization begins shortly after launch and concludes with Roman entering its halo orbit around L2.

Roman will soon join our James Webb Space Telescope at the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), located 1 million miles away. At L2, the gravity of the Sun and Earth, together with an object’s motion around the Sun, let it stay lined up with Earth as they orbit, allowing Roman to have a relatively steady orbit without using much fuel.

content.alt_text: Eight people pose with celebratory posters in front of a large countdown clock set at -26 minutes. They are smiling and looking excited. The posters all have congratulatory messages for the mission. Credit: NASA/Jamie Adkins

content.text: Attendees at the Roman launch NASA social shared their excitement in the lead-up to launch.

Seven minutes after launch, the ground control team at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, began receiving telemetry data from Roman. The Falcon Heavy rocket performed as expected, separating from the observatory 31 minutes into the flight. After separating from the center core, the rocket’s side boosters safely returned to the launch site for refurbishment.

This artist’s concept animation shows Roman’s deployment sequence once in space. First, the solar panels and sunshade deploy to shade the rest of the observatory and begin providing electrical power. Then the antenna boom arm swings out with the communications dish attached. Finally, the visor-like deployable aperture cover lifts up to reveal the primary mirror underneath.

In the coming hours, the observatory’s solar panels and lower instrument Sun shade will deploy. Within days, Roman’s high-gain antenna and visor-like deployable aperture cover will deploy, ground controllers will initiate the first of two-mid-course corrections, and the Coronagraph Instrument will power on.

This instrument will demonstrate the technology that future missions like our Habitable Worlds Observatory could use to image Earth-like planets. Roman’s Coronagraph will take a giant step in that direction by snapping pictures of Jupiter-like planets.

content.alt_text: A pale yellow grid of three arched rows appears in the lower left on a black background. Two more stack above it, and then three orange ones appear alongside them in the middle of the screen. Three more in a deeper orange color appear along those on the right side of the screen, and then the entire group of 18 arched grids is copied over the top of them multiple times at different angles. Credit: NASA

content.text: This sequence shows how Roman will conduct some of its observations to view the same region multiple times. That will help scientists see things that change over time, like exploding stars and snacking black holes.

A few weeks into Roman’s voyage, its primary instrument — the Wide Field Instrument — will activate. This 300-megapixel infrared camera has 18 4K detectors, each about the size of a saltine cracker. These detectors collect photons of light that will be decoded into crisp cosmic panoramas. With its large view, Roman will survey the universe hundreds of times faster than NASA’s Hubble or James Webb space telescopes can.

content.embed_html: <iframe width="356" height="200"  id="youtube_iframe" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/FkgVB19I6xw?feature=oembed&enablejsapi=1&origin=https://safe.txmblr.com&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="NASA's Roman Space Telescope: A New Perspective on the Cosmos (Official NASA Trailer)"></iframe>

attribution.display_text: NASA - NASA's Roman Space Telescope: A New Perspective on the Cosmos (Official NASA Trailer)

content.text: Throughout the rest of Roman’s three-month commissioning period, scientists will run the instruments through a series of calibrations and tests. NASA anticipates releasing Roman’s first images by early 2027.
Rewatch the Roman launch here and follow along with Roman’s journey to L2 at science.nasa.gov/blogs/roman.

content.text: Four Mysterious Space Rabbit Holes to Fall Down

content.alt_text: Mysterious Space Rabbit Holes to Fall Down is written in thick white font over a video flying through a deep field image. Yellow and white dots, which are galaxies, sail toward the camera and then fly past, growing larger. Some are distinguishable spiral shapes as they get closer. It’s all set against the black of space. Credit: NASA, ESA, F. Summers, J. DePasquale, G. Bacon, and Z. Levay (STScI)

content.text: Need a break from mindlessly scrolling?
Take a deep dive into some mysterious space rabbit holes, curated by us, for you. Bizarre enough to keep you locked in, and we’ve got a starter point for each topic.

content.alt_text: Dark Matter is written in thick white font over a Hubble image. Space is black. White, yellow, and light blue galaxies dot the entire image. The center of the image has a yellow glow, illuminated by especially bright yellow galaxies. Above and to the left of the yellow glow, three blue spiral galaxies are large enough to see the arms. Credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Postman, P. Kelly

content.text: Dark Matter
When we say “dark,” we mean mysterious.
We think ordinary matter makes up only about 5% of the universe, while dark matter makes up about 27%, including most of the mass of galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Dark matter is invisible, but it takes up space and it holds mass, so it interacts with and influences ordinary matter gravitationally, which makes it possible to study. Our brand new Roman space telescope will investigate dark matter like never before.
Dive into dark matter: https://science.nasa.gov/dark-matter/

content.alt_text: Rogue Planets is written in thick white text over an artist’s concept of a rogue planet in space. The background of space is black, but dotted with thousands of tiny white stars and galaxies, which give a dark blue cast. From the center middle to the lower right, a Milky Way like galaxy runs in a purple and red diagonal line. A planet, very dimly lit, is crossing in front of the line of galaxy. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/R. Hurt (Caltech-IPAC)

content.text: Rogue Planets

Exoplanets are planets outside our solar system. Some exoplanets exist without a planetary system…at all. These planets don’t orbit a star but float freely through space. Following previous missions, the Roman space telescope will help find hundreds of rogue planets, which can help us understand how planetary systems form…and how planets exist without systems.
Go rogue: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/rogue-planets/

content.alt_text: Saturn’s Hexagon is written in thick white font over a grayscale Cassini image of Saturn’s north pole. The upper edge of the planet fills most of the right side of the frame, seen at an angle. A darker gray hexagon covers the topmost region of Saturn, with an even darker circle at its center. In the background, light gray rings stand out against the black of space. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute

content.text: Saturn’s Hexagon Jet Stream

First spotted by the Voyager spacecraft, the hexagon at Saturn’s north pole was a mystery for decades. It seemed like a jet stream, but jet streams on Earth are wobbly and irregular, unlike Saturn’s neatly geometric crown. Further missions to Saturn and research on Earth found that in a deep, uniform atmosphere without landforms like mountains to churn it up, jet streams can form bizarrely neat geometric shapes.
See the shape on Saturn: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/cassini/science/saturn/hexagon-in-motion/

content.alt_text: Little Red Dots is written in thick white text over the left half of a Webb image of a galaxy cluster that includes a little red dot, visible three times due to gravitational lensing. Dozens of white, yellow, orange, and red galaxies stand out against the black of space. In the center of the image, several white galaxies are surrounded by a hazy white glow. Three small boxes run in an arc through these central glowing galaxies, from about 12 o’clock to 4 o’clock. They are labeled C, B, and A, starting from the top. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Lukas Furtak (Ben-Gurion University); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI)

content.text: Little Red Dots

Little Red Dots, first found in Webb telescope data, are mysterious compact objects that appear about 600 million years after the big bang, and seem to decline about a billion years later - but new data show that perhaps they didn't disappear, they evolved. Are they indeed a form of supermassive black hole, potentially obscured by gas or dust?
Spot Little Red Dots: https://science.nasa.gov/missions/chandra/nasa-connects-little-red-dots-with-chandra-webb/

summary: Four Mysterious Space Rabbit Holes to Fall Down

content.text: Maybe I should write that post about how I got an extra sensory input from a high pitch noise in really fucking broken Mercedes 190E. After I fixed the problem, I had the worst migraine in my life after driving the said car for 1 hour, because my brain could not adapt to the fact that "oh, this high pitch sound that was directly correlated to the current speed and some other parameters is now gone".

I could genuinely drive that thing without ever looking at the instrument cluster, because I could intuitively infer all necessary values from that auditory input. No other car ever felt so personal. I've built a brain-shitbox-interface and I've lost it.

My first time operating CCTV cameras I was handed control over what was essentially 50 independently moving eyes that collectively covered an area about the size of a football field and from that experience I now know that
Suddenly having 50 moving eyes can make you disoriented and barfy and the adjustment period sucks ass
It takes both more and less time than you’d think to figure out what the structure as a whole looks like and where those eyes ARE

After you get used to it the entirety of the structure itself and all of the eyes you can see from feels like an extension of your nervous system in a very bizarre way. Like I have dreams now from the perspective of A Building and I’m not sure how to describe that.
Once you are aware of an unreachable blind spot it nags at you constantly and you can feel it like a hard little lump under your skin you need to poke and scratch at and it’s ardghgguychgghhbhhhbhhh

And on top of that, having operated CCTV at multiple locations now- my favourite and most comfortable one having excess of 60 cameras- it can be REALLY hard to suddenly jump to a different operating interface and display configuration, because all the muscle memory is wrong

On my COMFORTABLE system, the one I spent the longest time on, I never had to think about what code I needed to punch in. If I needed to watch a specific person, I could follow them all over the site without thinking about it.

Now at a different location, all the manual equipment and codes and lag and resolution are different, and it feels like going from playing the piano to driving stick shift on the left side of the road with my feet
The closest I imagine I can equate it to is like. Getting really really good at painting with a pair of prosthetic hands, and then suddenly having them swapped out with someone else’s
Not the best depiction, but. Feels like this

content.text: There this understanding of Transmasc/Transfem that is not an identity per say but the way you transition from your asab and more importantly how you are seen by society not your personal identity. So. A feminine enby who uses they/them is transmasc bc they are transition away from femininity and “femaleness” ; vice versa for a butch transfem with they/them pronouns. This is why many nonbinary ppl who were CAMAB see themselves as transfem regardless if they see themselves as women/or fem-aligned bc the world sees themselves as trans women and thus affected by transmisogyny.
Idk how to think of it bc I do understand  where they are coming from. I
Oh yeah, that's a very common misconception outside of the nonbinary community about the use of transition labels! I'm happy to explain.

First off, the transmasc/transfem labels have evolved over time. They started gaining traction in the early 2000s — although they had existed since at least the '90s — and were used as a catch-all term for anyone who was trans, without having to necessarily identify as transsexual or binary transgender. Like many historical labels, they have existed for most of their history as nebulous terms with no set definition, just a general vibe.

To start, I want to note that some of the earlier attempts at defining those labels did try to describe them in terms of what one is transitioning away from, instead of what one's actual gender identity is.
For example, advocate S. Leigh Thompson (who is a trans man) proposed this definition in 2006:
Transmasculine: Any person who was assigned female at birth but feels that is an incomplete or incorrect description of their gender.

That being said, those sorts of definitions never really became the predominant ones inside of nonbinary communities. And as of right now, they are actively disliked by most. For one, they don't take into account intersex people, who might have a complex history with gender and might use "contradictory" labels like AFAB transfem or AMAB transmasc. Furthermore, those definitions just.. don't make sense from a nonbinary perspective. Which is a big problem, since the labels transfem/transmasc are supposed to be used to include (some of) us.

Those definitions stem from the exorsexist idea that there is only one possible direction of transition: away from your "biological sex" and towards the "opposite sex". But gender is more complex than a line that goes from "man" to "woman" in which getting away from "man" necessarily pushes you towards "woman" and vice versa. For example, a medically-transitioning transneutral person might wish to remove their gendered characteristics (breasts, facial hair, etc.), but not wish to gain the ones associated with the opposite sex, like a binary-aligned trans person typically would. Even though they are transitioning away from typical presentations of their assigned sex-gender, their transition is also atypical for transfems/transmascs norms, and categorizing them as either of those just based on their AGAB would be reductive. Not to mention that social transition (being recognized as one's actual gender by society) is an integral part of transitioning, too. Categorizing a trans person as transmasc or transfem when they don't consider their gender identity masculine nor feminine is basically misgendering. At the end of the day, you (general you) are still telling someone who sees themselves as neutral, or androgynous, or fluid, or anything else they might identity as, that they need to be categorized based on the gender binary.

This framework also leads to the false idea that nonbinary people will always have more in common with binary trans people of the same "biological sex" than a nonbinary person of the "opposite" one with a similar gender identity. This is simply not the case, and in nonbinary spaces we rarely divide ourselves based on AGAB. A transmasculine or transfeminine enban might feel understood and included in trans man/woman spaces, but that's because they are transitioning towards masculinity/femininity just like them, not because AGAB inherently creates a connection between trans people. I, for one, feel a lot more understood amongst other neutral/unaligned people than I do around more binary-aligned people with my same AGAB.

Now, there are people who, despite being told all of this, will still argue in favor of using the labels in the way you (asker) have observed from others. Often under the guise of "society at large is transphobic and doesn't recognize nonbinary genders, so your oppression can only be described accurately if the labels indicate what you're transitioning away from". And my question to them is: if society is transphobic and doesn't recognize me as my actual gender, shouldn't a trans advocacy movement strive to change that, instead of telling trans people their identity doesn't exist? Furthermore: why does transness always need to be defined in terms of suffering? Why should an identity label be assigned to me based on how society (mis)treats me, instead of giving me the agency to choose the words to describe my own experience?

And, if you allow me to be petty for a second, the trans people arguing for using transfem and transmasc in that way are exhibiting a real "rules for thee but not for me" attitude. Because if someone said "trans women and trans men are not recognized as their actual genders by society at large, so we're going to use these labels that actively misgender them to describe their transition" they would, rightfully, lose their minds. But when it comes to nonbinary people, it's suddenly fine to force us in gendered categories that don't match our actual gender, based entirely on our AGAB. It's a double standard, and antithetical to what trans advocacy should stand for.

At the end of the day, enben deserve to have words to describe our transition without forcibly binarizing us and our experiences. This is why we have labels such as transneutral and transandrogynous, and sometimes I wonder if more people would identify with them if they were more widely known and widely accepted.

Our identities and our language shouldn't revolve around what bigots think of us. To circle back to the example you brought up: an unaligned nonbinary person should be able to say "I'm unaligned and I've faced a lot of transmisogyny in my life" and be taken seriously, without their identity being called into question, without having to disclose their AGAB to "prove it", and without having to adopt the transfem label (if it doesn't resonate with them) just to be included. Unfortunately, as it currently is, a lot of us feel like we have to binarize our identity in order to receive solidarity.
I hope this explains it, and I'm glad you brought up the topic, anon! I have been meaning to talk about this for a while.

content.text: Land of The Giants Project for Iceland
This design transforms mundane electrical pylons into statues on the Icelandic landscape.Choi + Shine,is the US architecture practice behind the proposal

Making only minor alterations to well established  steel-framed tower design, we have created a series of towers that are  powerful, solemn and variable. These iconic pylon-figures will become  monuments in the landscape. Seeing the pylon-figures will become an  unforgettable experience, elevating the towers to something more than  merely a functional design of necessity.

The pylon-figures can be  configured to respond to their environment with appropriate gestures.   As the carried electrical lines ascend a hill, the pylon-figures change  posture, imitating a climbing person. Over long spans, the pylon-figure  stretches to gain increased height, crouches for increased strength or  strains under the weight of the wires.

The pylon-figures can also be arranged to create a sense of place  through deliberate expression. Subtle alterations in the hands and head  combined with repositioning of the main body parts in the x, y and  z-axis, allow for a rich variety of expressions. The pylon-figures can  be placed in pairs, walking in the same direction or opposite  directions, glancing at each other as they pass by or kneeling  respectively, head bowed at a town.

Like the statues of Easter Island, it is envisioned  that these one hundred and fifty foot tall, modern caryatids will take  on a quiet authority, belonging to their landscape yet serving the  people, silently transporting electricity across all terrain, day and  night, sunshine or snow.

content.text: each morning

each morning around dawn 
one of our phones makes one of those noises
or my watch vibrates or the baby rhino-sized radiator 
cracks its back and makes the house shake. each time, 
I try to fall back into sleep, desperate to live in a dream(or 
nothing) for an hour more, knowing the pandemic will wait, 
won't allow me to miss anything.

after a few minutes I yield to middle-age, 
throw off the covers in an explosion of crackle and sparks 
from the charged(+/-)particles settled and taken refuge about us 
overnight. and I fall back into the world(important: both feet 
must land together) I want to be anywhere this morning 
but in my mind. I walk past the children's rooms, close-click 
their doors and step carefully onto the old stairs to preserve the quiet,

the dog quietly approaches and understands
I will ignore her until water boils 
and beans are obliterated.

summary: each morning

content.text: how did we come to lie here

how did we come to lie here?
among the wet stones, rusted 
fences meant to keep us 
in or out of the world. either way 
they offend us. pick up a rock, I say, 
and we'll play a game.

how did we come to lie here 
on our backs, with eyes shut against the light?
I feel for your hand. getting warmer, warmer 
you say. I am hungry and this hunger is a circle 
we can't step out of. listen, I can hear the circle 
now it hums and far in the beautiful(beautiful) 
distance we hear our children, and we can go back 
to sleep for a little while longer.

summary: how did we come to lie here

content.text: the image(of)the image

we are not after truths. we are after the image of truths. 
we are safer in the image of the image of truths. what we know 
is forgettable and what we don't know we live our lives scared 
to forget. we are in a place between forgettable knowledge 
and forfeited knowledge. no door of any width, no squeeze of any heart
will free us. once we are gone once
we are no more less than we were. from nothing to never 
silence shame. we see only the image 
of wounds, and the image of the image
of unforgiving fathers, slow-dying
in firelight.

summary: the image(of)the image

content.text: 20th

AM
no waking things to wake us yet.
and just as well, since our dreams
haven't fully receded, pooling
at the backs of our eyes, 
in the same manner that nightfrost 
drips from the tips of the atlas spruce 
in the heat of morning. i reach for you 
and gather up the light.

PM
quickly, with careful fingers
you reach into the sound of a chainsaw
and rearrange it. even before
you draw back your hand,
I hear swallows. you repeat the act,
now it's a chorus of cicadas.

a gust shakes seedcopters 
out of the maple across the street.
they fall spinning, with a metallic whine i find
unbearable, and land like bolts on the asphalt.

but you, 
you are hearing the molecules
of paint on our porch deck sing
in the stillstrong sunlight.

summary: 20th

content.text: Mistborn: Secret History by Brandon Sanderson is like meeting an old friend after a long time. 4.75/5

I have done my best to avoid spoilers for the era 2 of Mistborn so I didn't know what to expect from this. And it was a pleasant surprise. I wholeheartedly recommend this to everyone who has already read the Mistborn-trilogy (ergo, era 1), as it fills in some gaps left by the books and gives further context to what happened during the main trilogy.

The book differs slightly from Sanderson's other works, the setting and point-of-view of the main character are somewhat abstract, and time occasionally difficult to follow —which isn't a negative thing but rather brings a mysterious air to the story. It also further expands the overall mystery of the Cosmere, not just the world of the Mistborn but expanding to Sanderson's other books as well. (I still maintain my previously stated opinion that it is not necessary for anyone to do "homework", though.)

content.text: There are 4 sednoids and all of them are funny
The sednoids are objects with extremely wide orbits around the sun. Here's a diagram:
There are 4 sednoids. Sedna, 2023 KQ14 (nicknamed "Ammonite"), 2012 VP113 (nicknamed "Biden") and lastly but certainly not least Leleākūhonua (originally nicknamed "The Goblin").

Leleākūhonua was nicknamed "The Goblin" due to being discovered near to Halloween and also being given a designation with the letters "TG" in it, which the discoverers thought it would be funny to turn into "The Goblin". 2012 VP113 was nicknamed "Biden" since Joe Biden was the VP of the US at the time. Also hilarious.

Most sednoids look like this. That's the best photos we have since they're so far away. We have no clue why they orbit so far away from the sun. There's a few theories, most notably a ninth planet distorting their orbits, but we can't be certain. There also could be many more beyond our ability to see. Since they orbit extremely slowly (10000 years for one orbit of Sedna), there could be many at their furthest points away from the sun that we have never discovered. Isn't that weird?

summary: There are 4 sednoids and all of them are funny

content.text: The Secret to Smooth Skin Using Everyday Natural Ingredients [Step-by-Step]
The Hidden Truth about Our Daily Face Struggles

Waking up and avoiding the bathroom mirror became my daily routine for years. My face was constantly red, irritated, and covered in angry breakouts, no matter how many expensive creams I bought. Eventually, I stopped listening to flashy beauty aids and started focusing on real skin health. Let me share the completely natural approach to skin care that finally gave me the glowing, smooth skin I always wanted without breaking the bank.

I remember looking in the mirror one morning and feeling completely defeated by my own reflection. My face looked tired, dull, and honestly, a bit angry at me for everything I was putting it through. I had tried dozens of expensive bottles promising a glowing look, but absolutely nothing worked for me. I spent hours reading online forums, buying into every new trend that popped up on my social media feed. My bathroom cabinet looked like a small pharmacy, yet my actual skin health was getting worse every single day.
I finally realized that my body did not need more complex chemicals; it simply needed a break. I decided to strip everything back and focus entirely on a pure, natural approach to skin care.

So many of us wake up feeling deeply frustrated about our daily appearance. You wash your face, apply heavy layers of expensive products, and still notice dry patches or unexpected breakouts by noon. It feels like a never-ending battle that completely drains your physical energy and your hard-earned money.

The sad truth is that we are constantly overwhelming our faces with harsh, unforgiving synthetic ingredients. We expect instant miracles from artificial formulas, totally forgetting that our bodies respond best to what nature provides. Dealing with constant irritation leaves you feeling physically uncomfortable and mentally exhausted all day long.

content.text: Testing an antenna layout for the SKA-Low telescope
On-sky observations confirm a predicted sensitivity loss at 125 MHz, informing the antenna layout for SKA-Low

SKA-Low is a radio telescope under construction in Western Australia. It will operate across a wide frequency range, from 50 to 350 MHz, and will be the most sensitive telescope of its kind ever built. The completed instrument will link 512 individual stations spread across an area roughly 75 km wide. Each station's antennas work together like a single large dish, so the way those antennas are arranged directly shapes what the telescope can detect.

An earlier prototype station, AAVS2, arranged its antennas in a scattered, pseudo-random pattern to avoid unwanted signal artifacts. But antennas placed too close together can interfere with one another, a problem known as mutual coupling. This interference grows stronger below about 150 MHz, squarely within SKA-Low's operating range.

To fix this, researchers within the Observatory proposed a new arrangement inspired by the spiral pattern seen in sunflower heads, known as the Vogel layout. Spacing the antennas this way reduces interference between neighbors while preserving the station's collecting power. The SKA Observatory built a new prototype station, AAVS3, using this layout to test it under real sky conditions.

As reported in the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems, researchers led by Dr. Shin'ichiro Asayama of the SKA Observatory describe how they built and tested AAVS3, and what the results mean for the telescope's final design. The team combined computer simulations with real observations to check the station's sensitivity and calibration accuracy. AAVS3 uses 256 dual-polarized antennas and was tested both as a signal-combining beamformer and as an imaging array. The researchers pointed it at the Sun, bright cosmic radio sources, the Galactic Plane, and several pulsars.

They also built two ways to calibrate the station, essentially the process of correcting the raw data so it accurately reflects the sky. The simpler method used the Sun as a known reference point. The second, more thorough approach combined the Sun with a sky-brightness model and detailed antenna response profiles, and unlike the Sun-only method, it also worked at night.

Simulations run while AAVS3 was being built predicted a loss of sensitivity directly overhead at around 125 MHz. The team traced this to repeated antenna spacings, about 2.4 meters apart, that occur throughout the sunflower pattern and create interference patterns that reduce sensitivity. Older prototype AAVS2, with its scattered layout, showed no such problem.

Real sky observations confirmed the prediction. When the Galactic Plane passed directly overhead, images clearly showed the same dip in sensitivity at 125 MHz. This confirmed the problem was a built-in consequence of the antenna geometry, not a flaw in the equipment or method.

The team separately checked the station's sensitivity at 230 MHz. At night, actual measurements closely matched predictions when using the more thorough calibration method. Daytime measurements showed larger gaps from predictions, most likely because unusually high solar activity during the observations made the Sun's brightness harder to predict accurately.

Because of the sensitivity loss at 125 MHz, engineers ruled out the original sunflower layout for the finished telescope. Further simulations led them to a modified version, called "Perturbed Vogel," which keeps antennas spaced to avoid interference while removing the repeating pattern that caused the problem. Testing this new layout falls outside the current study.

The AAVS3 results give SKA-Low's teams practical guidance for building and calibrating the actual stations in the construction phase. Combined with lessons from AAVS2, this work has directly shaped the observatory's testing process and supported a key construction milestone, known as AA0.5, marking the first stations to come online.

The Vogel pattern maximizes spacing between antennas to reduce interference, but on-sky tests revealed a sensitivity loss at 125 MHz that led the Observatory to select a different layout for the final telescope. content.text: Astronomers uncover black hole jets reaching far beyond their galaxies and deciding their fate

Galaxies are enormous and hold hundreds of billions of stars. These stars form from cold, dense gas. Indeed, every large galaxy, including the Milky Way, is wrapped in a huge envelope of gas called the circumgalactic medium, or CGM. This gas is a reservoir of raw material and stretches 10-20 times the size of the visible portion of the galaxy. This CGM gas eventually cools, moves inward into the galaxy, and clumps together to form stars. Thus, the CGM plays a key role in shaping stars, planets, and even life within a galaxy. But astronomers have long puzzled over why, given how much star-forming gas surrounds them, galaxies don't have even more stars. What is keeping the fuel from cooling down and forming those stars?

A new study led by astronomers Sanchayeeta Borthakur of Arizona State University (ASU) and Namrata Roy, now at the Raman Research Institute (RRI), found evidence that narrow jets of heated plasma, blasted out by the supermassive black holes at galaxies' centers, can affect the whole galaxy even beyond what we can see, and may shape its future. The jets may reach out and disrupt the gas that galaxies need to keep growing. Their research has been published in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.

“This is a pathbreaking result that solves the long-standing mystery of how black holes influence galaxies, their stars, and life as we know it!” said Borthakur, Associate Professor in ASU’s School of Earth and Space Exploration. “This work opens a new direction to explore further the intricacies of the connection between the supermassive black holes trillions of miles from where we are to how we came to be here.”
Little in size, big in influence

When a black hole actively feeds on gas, it can release enormous energy that heats the surrounding gas. Even though these black holes can be powerhouses of energy, they are quite small and are roughly about the size of our solar system. On the other hand, their host galaxies can hold about 100 billion such solar systems.
“The surprising question is: how can something so small energetically impact something so enormous?” said Roy, assistant professor at RRI and former ASU Exploration Prize Postdoctoral Fellow.

One way to envision it is to think of an ant leaving its impression hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. Scientists still do not fully understand how energy from these active black holes reaches such distances and changes along the way.

The team’s study provides evidence as to how this could occur. They focused on active black holes that emit strong jets, which are narrow streams of hot, fast-moving plasma shooting out far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge. They looked for a distinct imprint in the ionization state of the gaseous reservoir caused by these jets. The ionized gas, or the “glow” from hydrogen gas they were looking for in the CGM, is so faint that no single galaxy would show it clearly. Hence, the team combined observations of hundreds of galaxies with active jets, using data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey and radio jet measurements from the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey (LoTSS). They combined measurements coming from the direction of the jet axes and searched for a specific telltale sign of ionized hydrogen gas along the jet path, known as H-alpha.

Roy, Borthkur and colleagues showed that when averaged over all directions around the galaxies, the signal was weak; however, along the radio jets, the H-alpha signal became clear and strong. This indicates that the gas does not glow uniformly everywhere but is particularly bright along the jet path. A simple analogy is that the jet acts less like a lamp shining in all directions, and more like a powerful beam that makes the gas glow where it passes through.

These findings show that black-hole jets do not affect the gas surrounding galaxies equally in all directions; instead, they leave a distinct impression by causing the gas to shine and become ionized mainly along the radio jet's path. They also found that the jets have the biggest impact, and that the glow from ionized hydrogen is brightest in two places: close to the galaxy where the jet first hits the CGM, and much farther out near the CGM’s outer edge, where the jet releases most of its energy. This provides a clear signature of how jets can illuminate or disrupt the surrounding gas, even at great distances, all the way to the CGM. This mechanism helps shape the galaxy's environment, influence its growth and evolution - it determines whether the galaxy continues to form stars or becomes quiescent.

“What excites me most is the scale of the connection,” Roy said. “A black hole is incredibly small compared to a galaxy, but its impact can reach hundreds of thousands of light-years, far into the galaxy’s outer reaches. The jet carries the energy outward, and the gas lights up along its path.

”As a check, the team also examined a tracer of cooler gas via the absorption signature of magnesium. Unlike the directional glow in H-alpha, Magnesium was more widely distributed isotropically and did not show any connection to the jet direction. This implies that the cool gas component might already exist as a reservoir surrounding the galaxy uniformly on all sides. Yet the jet brightens, heats, and ionizes gas along its own path, lighting up a trail and causing it to glow in H-alpha.
Black holes determine a galaxy's fate.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet for how a black hole can affect galaxies far beyond its central region. By heating, stirring, and disturbing gas throughout the CGM, jets can prevent that gas from cooling down and falling inward to fuel new stars. This acts as a brake on the galaxy’s growth, changes its fate, and makes it much less active in star formation.
This means the black hole is not just “feeding” at the center of the galaxy, as some might think. It also reaches out and changes the galaxy’s environment, which can eventually change its fate.
Specific Directions: Look both ways on the path

Past studies searched for the signal but couldn't detect it, making this directional discovery an exciting breakthrough. The signal only appears when we look along the jet direction. If the astronomers had thought the CGM was the same in every direction, the team would have missed this discovery. The jet ionizes hydrogen gas along its path, making it glow in H-alpha in a very specific direction.

This study shows the value of large optical and radio surveys like the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey and the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey (LoTss). By combining many weak signals, astronomers can now study the behavior of galaxies that would otherwise stay hidden. The study also gives astronomers and theorists a new way to test how black-hole jets affect galaxies.

IMAGE: Artist’s illustration of a supermassive black hole at the center of a radio galaxy launching powerful jets (shown in pink) all the way into the galaxy’s CGM. The study finds that these jets do not light up the surrounding gas equally in all directions. Instead, the hydrogen gas glows (shown in red) most strongly along the path of the radio jets. This suggests that black holes can send energy far beyond the galaxy’s center and shape the larger gas reservoir that regulates star formation and fate of galaxies. We use optical data from the DESI survey and radio  observations from the LOFAR Two meter Sky Survey (LoTss). Credit Image courtesy of Hailey Nelson/ Arizona State University.

summary: Astronomers uncover black hole jets reaching far beyond their galaxies and deciding their fate

content.text: Early galaxies were already seeding the universe with heavy elements
Early galaxies were already seeding the cosmos with heavy elements, such as oxygen and carbon, just 500 million years after the Big Bang

When the universe was still in its infancy – only 500 million years after the Big Bang or about 3% of its current age – some of the universe's earliest stars and galaxies had already formed. Astronomers have long predicted that much of the gas surrounding these young galaxies must have remained rather pristine, composed of mostly hydrogen and helium, the primordial ingredients available in the newborn cosmos.

According to a study published by astronomers at the University of Arizona in Nature Astronomy, this picture likely is not correct. Instead, galaxies were already seeding the cosmos with heavy elements, such as oxygen and carbon, much earlier than astronomers expected.

"We observed that heavy elements escaped from galaxies very, very early in cosmic time," said Yongda Zhu, first author of the paper and postdoctoral researcher at the U of A Department of Astronomy and Steward Observatory. "Not only were the galaxies producing these elements, but they were also dispersing them, possibly seeding other galaxies."
How the universe got its elements

In the early universe, the cosmos barely contained anything other than hydrogen and helium, the two simplest elements occupying the very top of the periodic table. Over time, gravity pulled clouds of these simple elements together to form stars, where the immense pressures and temperatures inside allowed nuclear fusion and other reactions to forge more complex, heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen.

When stars burned out or ended their lives as supernovae, they shed these heavy elements into space, where they became the building blocks for future generations of stars, planets and ultimately, life. Even the carbon in our bodies and the oxygen we breathe were forged in earlier generations of stars.
Until now, however, it wasn't clear how and when heavier elements were transported from the earliest galaxies into the surrounding universe.
Looking at early galaxies

Zhu's research centered on three early galaxies whose light has traveled for more than 13 billion years, showing them as they appeared about 500 million years after the Big Bang, during a cosmic period known as the Epoch of Reionization. At that time, the first generations of stars and galaxies were transforming the early universe by ionizing the hydrogen gas between them. This process, during which electrons were stripped from their hydrogen nuclei, gradually brought an end to the cosmic "dark ages" by allowing ultraviolet light to travel more freely through the universe.

"We used the galaxies themselves as background light sources," said Zhu. "As light from the galaxies traveled toward Earth, it passed through surrounding gas, and we were able to look at the light's absorption patterns to detect specific elements."

Observations of these ancient galaxies were only made possible by the infrared capabilities of NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, which allowed the researchers to observe galaxies as they appeared about 13 billion years ago. The nearly 30 hours of exposure provided enough light to detect faint absorption patterns in the spectra of these distant galaxies.

Over the course of one long night, Zhu manually searched through publicly available JWST spectra from hundreds of galaxies and pinpointed three with absorption patterns indicating the presence of heavy elements, including carbon, oxygen and silicon. The absorption lines were "blueshifted" relative to the galaxies' redshift, indicating that the gas was moving outward from the galaxies and carrying oxygen, carbon and other heavy elements into intergalactic space.

The chemical fingerprints of these infant galaxies closely resembled those of evolved galaxies billions of years later, providing evidence that even at cosmic dawn, galaxies were already producing and spreading heavy elements into the space around them.

"Think of these elements, which originated from the galaxies' stars, as food dye dropped into a cup of water," said Zhu. "The color begins to spread through the water, and, in a similar fashion, these heavy elements from early galaxies began to escape into space and 'enrich' their surroundings."
Baryon Cycling

The process by which galaxies exchange material is known as baryon cycling. It is one reason galaxies are not isolated systems, but interconnected parts of a larger galactic ecosystem. Material produced by one generation of stars can be recycled and redistributed through this galactic ecosystem.

The discovery of early baryon cycling may also help explain why astronomers have struggled to find the first generation of stars, known as Population III stars. These stars are thought to have been the very first stars formed from pristine gas containing only hydrogen and helium, before heavier elements had been produced and dispersed throughout the universe. If galaxies were already enriching their surroundings only 500 million years after the Big Bang, truly pristine gas – and the Population III stars that formed from it – simply may not have been around long enough to be observed.
"If you start out with pure vanilla ice cream but start mixing in sprinkles soon after, it won't be long until you can no longer find any pristine, plain, vanilla ice cream,” Zhu said.

IMAGE: Artist’s visualization of an early galaxy and its surrounding gaseous environment. The orange structures represent metal-enriched gas being expelled from the galaxy, illustrating how young galaxies began dispersing heavy elements into their surroundings within the Universe’s first 500 million years. The visualization is based on publicly available FIRE-2 cosmological simulation data and is not a direct telescope image. Credit Yongda Zhu
